draft.title: International competitiveness
card: International competitiveness is how well Australian goods and services compete with those of other countries, on price and on quality. A competitive economy can sell more exports and win more of its home market from imports.
Productivity and costs
Higher labour productivity means more output per worker, which lowers the cost of each unit. Lower wages, energy and other input costs also let firms sell at lower prices.
Resources and inflation

Natural resources such as minerals and good farmland give some industries a lasting advantage. If Australian inflation is lower than that of trading partners, our prices fall relative to theirs, which improves competitiveness.
Exchange rate
A lower exchange rate makes Australian goods cheaper in foreign currency, which improves price competitiveness. A higher rate makes them dearer overseas and so weakens it.
draft.remember: Competitiveness improves when Australian goods become better value, through lower relative prices or better quality.

a.q: Which change would most clearly improve the price competitiveness of Australian manufacturers?
opts: A rise in output per worker that cuts the cost of each unit
A rise in the Australian dollar against trading partners
Australian inflation rising above that of trading partners
A rise in the energy and input costs paid by manufacturers
a.why: More output per worker lowers unit costs, so firms can charge less. A higher dollar makes goods dearer overseas, and higher relative inflation and higher input costs raise prices, so those three weaken competitiveness.
a.clue: Which change lets firms charge less for each unit?

b.q: A Ballarat wine exporter sells in Japan. The Australian dollar falls against the yen, and its prices in Australian dollars do not change. What happens to its competitiveness in Japan?
opts: It improves, as the wine costs fewer yen
It weakens, as the wine costs more yen
It is unchanged, as its Australian prices are the same
It weakens, as the lower dollar shows lower quality
b.why: Each yen buys more Australian dollars, so the same wine costs Japanese buyers fewer yen. Its price falls relative to rivals, so competitiveness improves. The price in Australian dollars being unchanged does not matter to Japanese buyers.
b.clue: Think about the price Japanese buyers pay in yen.

a.best: A rise in output per worker that cuts the cost of each unit

b.best: It improves, as the wine costs fewer yen

problems.detail: The right option is the longest and the only one that explains its own effect ('that cuts the cost of each unit'). It also echoes the clue ('charge less for each unit'), so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.
